People in Ukraine are being killed every day by missiles, bombs, and drones . But the country's central and southeastern European neighbors have also found themselves affected, albeit on a smaller scale: Missiles and drones sometimes invade their air space, and occasionally even crash on their territory. Now the Russian drone war is coming dangerously close to two of Ukraine's neighbors: Romania and the Republic of Moldova , where drone incidents are now an almost daily occurrence. The drones often explode, leaving people injured, and there have also been recent attacks on Ukrainian checkpoints at the Moldovan and Romanian borders. Asked what's at stake for Europe in Sunday’s vote, Kristersson said: “I would say security policy. stories.article_text_excerpt: Turkish police arrested a British tourist in the southern resort of Alanya for allegedly spitting on the Turkish flag, media reports said Wednesday.The 58-year-old tourist argued with staff in a hotel then allegedly turned and spat on a flag hanging in the lobby, DHA and IHA news agencies reported, without specifying when it happened.Staff reported the man to police, who detained him and took him to the Alanya courthouse where he was formally arrested on charges of insulting or degrading a symbol of the Turkish state.He was remanded in custody and taken to a local prison just outside the city.There was no immediate response from the British embassy.Under Article 300 of the Turkish penal code, it is illegal to publicly disrespect the Turkish flag -- an offence that can carry a jail term of up to three years.In August 2025, prosecutors opened a criminal investigation into a tourist from Bosnia and Herzegovina for performing a pole dance on a Turkish flagpole in Cappadocia which she posted on social media.The outcome of the case was not clear.

stories.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
stories.summary: Traffickers are making big bucks smuggling millions of critically endangered eels across continents, using suitcases on planes and legal loopholes to deliver them to dinnerplates. Where are the smuggling hotspots?
stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JTSL Unai Eizaguirre, an eel fisherman for 30 years, prepares gear with a colleague in the Basque Country Image: Nicole Ris/DW Advertisement In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades. The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species , which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in illegally caught eels. "So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said Unai Eizaguirre who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls.
